Benzene and its relatives — the ring system found in a majority of drug molecules. This module covers aromaticity, Hückel's rule, benzene's structure, nomenclature, and the electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) reactions that define arene chemistry.

blocks.x: Importance of aromatic compounds

Many drugs are aromatic compounds. Knowledge of aromatic chemistry helps to understand the chemical nature, physical properties, stability, pharmacological actions, and toxicities of a majority of drug molecules. As one lecture slide puts it: “Every interesting drug molecule contains a substituted benzene ring somewhere.”
Everyday applications
Perfumes & fragrances, pharmaceuticals, food flavorings, dyes & pigments, polymers, and solvents.
Unusual stability
Benzene is highly unsaturated, yet unlike alkenes/alkynes/dienes it does not readily undergo addition (e.g. Br₂ gives no reaction with benzene, but reacts readily with ethylene).
Burn signature
Aromatic hydrocarbons have a relatively high C:H ratio, and burn with a strong, sooty, yellow flame.
Core definitions

Aromatic hydrocarbon (arene) A cyclic, planar, completely conjugated hydrocarbon whose ring system satisfies Hückel's rule. Benzene (C₆H₆) is the simplest example, isolated from coal gas in 1825 by Michael Faraday.

Hückel's rule (the 4th criterion for aromaticity) A cyclic, planar, completely conjugated compound is aromatic only if it contains 4n + 2 π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2…). Compounds meeting the first three criteria but containing 4n π electrons are especially unstable and are called antiaromatic.

Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) The characteristic reaction of aromatic rings: an electrophile, E⁺, substitutes for a ring hydrogen (ArH + E⁺ → ArE + H⁺), preserving the aromatic system rather than destroying it as an addition reaction would.
Directing effects Substituents already on a ring control both the orientation (ortho/para vs. meta) and the rate (activating vs. deactivating) of further EAS on that ring.
Cyclic+ Planar+ Conjugated+ 4n+2 π e⁻= Aromatic

blocks.x: The four criteria
Four structural criteria must ALL be satisfied for a compound to be classified as aromatic.
The molecule must be cyclic

Benzene (cyclic) is aromatic. 1,3,5-Hexatriene, despite having three alternating double bonds, is not aromatic because it is acyclic — there can be no p-orbital overlap between the two terminal carbons of an open chain.
The molecule must be planar

All adjacent p orbitals must be aligned so that π electron density can be delocalized. Cyclooctatetraene adopts a non-planar, tub-shaped conformation; its adjacent p orbitals cannot overlap, so it is not aromatic. Since it is non-planar, it reacts with Br₂ to give a simple addition product — just like other alkenes.
The molecule must be completely conjugated

Aromatic compounds must have a p orbital on every ring atom. 1,3-Cyclohexadiene has an sp³ CH₂ carbon with no p orbital; 1,3,5-cycloheptatriene likewise has one sp³ carbon breaking the conjugation. Neither is aromatic.
Hückel's rule

Hückel's rule An aromatic compound must contain 4n + 2 π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, and so forth — giving 2, 6, 10, 14…). Cyclic, planar, completely conjugated compounds containing 4n π electrons are especially unstable and are said to be antiaromatic.
Aromatic (4n+2)
Benzene: 6 π electrons. 4n+2 = 4(1)+2 = 6 → aromatic and especially stable.
Antiaromatic (4n)
Cyclobutadiene: 4 π electrons. 4n = 4(1) = 4 → antiaromatic and especially unstable.
Applying all four criteria at once

c: Non-aromatic — one sp³ ring carbon; not completely conjugated
Aromatic — every C is sp²; 10 (not 8 or 12) π electrons, 4n+2 (n=2)
Non-aromatic — non-planar (tub-shaped); 8 π electrons does not fit 4n+2

blocks.x: Aromatic, antiaromatic & heterocyclic 6π systems
C₆H₆ · the simplest arene
Benzene (C₆H₆) is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene), isolated from coal gas in 1825 by Michael Faraday.
The Kekulé hybrid

Benzene is often represented as a hybrid of two equivalent Kekulé structures. Each makes an equal contribution to the hybrid, so the C–C bonds are neither purely double nor purely single, but something in between — a “1½” bond.

Kekulé 1: C1=C2–C3=C4–C5=C6–(C1) ↔ Kekulé 2: C1–C2=C3–C4=C5–C6=(C1)
Neither structure alone is real — the true molecule is the resonance hybrid, with 6 delocalized π electrons spread evenly around the ring.
Bond angles & bond lengths
Shape
The carbon skeleton is a regular hexagon. Every C–C–C and H–C–C bond angle is 120°, consistent with sp² hybridization at each ring carbon.
Bond lengths
C–H ≈ 1.09 Å. C–C ≈ 1.39 Å uniformly around the ring — intermediate between a typical single (1.54 Å) and double (1.34 Å) C–C bond.
Hybridization & the π system

Each ring carbon is sp² hybridized: the 2s orbital mixes with two of the three 2p orbitals, leaving one unhybridized 2pᲥ orbital per carbon. This forms sp²–sp² σ bonds to neighbouring ring carbons and an sp²–1s σ bond to each hydrogen. The six leftover, unhybridized p orbitals — one per carbon, all perpendicular to the ring plane — overlap continuously around the ring, delocalizing the 6 π electrons above and below the plane.

blocks.title: Carbon's three hybridization states (sp³, sp², sp)

items: sp³: one 2s electron promoted into 2pế; 2s mixes with all three 2p orbitals → 4 equivalent sp³ orbitals (tetrahedral, e.g. methane).
sp²: 2s mixes with two of the three 2p orbitals, leaving one pure p orbital → trigonal planar geometry with a leftover p orbital for π bonding (benzene's ring carbons).
sp: 2s mixes with only one 2p orbital, leaving two pure p orbitals → linear geometry (e.g. alkynes).

blocks.x: Why benzene resists addition
Addition would require breaking the delocalized, highly stabilized aromatic π system — energetically unfavorable compared to substitution, which regenerates full aromaticity.
Benzenoid, polycyclic, macrocyclic & heterocyclic
Aromatic compounds fall into several structural families, from simple monocyclic benzenoids to heteroatom-containing rings.
The major classes
Benzenoid — monocyclic derivatives
Benzene and its single-ring derivatives: toluene (CH₃), phenol (OH), aniline (NH₂).
Benzenoid — polycyclic
Two or more fused six-membered aromatic rings: naphthalene (2 rings), anthracene (3 linear rings), phenanthrene, benzo[a]pyrene.
Nonbenzenoid
Aromatic rings not built purely from fused six-membered benzenoid rings, e.g. azulene (fused 5- and 7-membered rings).
Macrocyclic
Large, fully conjugated monocyclic rings satisfying Hückel's rule, e.g. [14]annulene.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs)

PAHs contain two or more fused aromatic rings and, like benzene, have multiple resonance contributing structures. Many PAHs are carcinogenic — benzo[a]pyrene (found in soot, tobacco smoke, and charred food) is a well-known example.
C₁₀H₈Naphthalene — 2 fused rings C₁₄H₁₀Anthracene — 3 linear rings C₁₄H₁₀Phenanthrene — 3 angular rings C₂₀H₁₂Benzo[a]pyrene — 5 rings, carcinogenic
Heterocyclic aromatics
Heterocyclic compound A compound that contains one or more atoms other than carbon (heteroatoms: nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, etc.) in its ring.
Heterocyclic aromatic compound A heterocyclic compound whose ring is aromatic. Pyridine and pyrimidine are heterocyclic analogs of benzene, each aromatic.

PYRIDINEC₅H₅N, 6-membered ring. The ring N is sp² hybridized. Its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital, perpendicular to the six 2p orbitals of the π system — so it is NOT part of the aromatic sextet, and remains available to act as a base.

PYRROLE5-membered ring, N–H. The N lone pair sits in a p orbital and IS part of the aromatic sextet (contributing 2 of the 6 π electrons) — making pyrrole nitrogen a much weaker base than pyridine nitrogen.
FURAN5-membered ring, O. One of oxygen's two lone pairs sits in a p orbital and is part of the aromatic sextet; the other sits in an sp² orbital and is not.

IMIDAZOLE5-membered ring, 2 N atoms. One N (N–H) contributes its lone pair to the aromatic sextet, like pyrrole; the other N (=N–) behaves like pyridine's N, with its lone pair available for basicity.
Rule of thumb: only a lone pair sitting in a p orbital, aligned with the ring's continuous π system, counts toward the Hückel 4n+2 total. A lone pair in an in-plane sp² (or sp³) orbital is excluded.
Common & systematic names
Provide common and systematic names of simple aromatic compounds and their derivatives.
Benzene as the parent name
In many simple compounds, benzene is the parent name and the substituent is simply indicated by a prefix.
C₆H₅FFluorobenzene C₆H₅ClChlorobenzene C₆H₅BrBromobenzene C₆H₅NO₂Nitrobenzene
Substituent + ring = a new parent name
Ortho, meta, para — and lowest locants

Locate substituents by lowest numbers, or use the classical locators ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-), and para (1,4-). Where one group imparts a special name, name the compound as a derivative of that molecule, with that carbon as C-1.
4-Bromotoluenep-Bromotoluene 3-Chloroanilinem-Chloroaniline 1,3-Dimethylbenzenem-Xylene 1-Chloro-4-ethylbenzenep-Chloroethylbenzene
Three or more substituents

items: With three or more substituents, number the atoms of the ring.
If one group imparts a special name, it becomes the parent name and that carbon is numbered C-1 (the other groups branch from there).
If no group imparts a special name, number to give the smallest set of locants, and list substituents alphabetically.

Phenyl vs. benzyl
Phenyl (Ph)
The benzene ring itself, used as a branch, attached directly (C₆H₅–). E.g. Ph–CH₂CH₂OH = 2-phenylethanol.
Benzyl (Bn)
A benzene ring with an additional CH₂ carbon as the branch point (Ph–CH₂–). E.g. PhCH₂Cl = benzyl chloride.
Substitution, not addition
The most characteristic reaction of aromatic compounds is substitution at a ring carbon.
Substitutions on the aromatic ring
Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS)

EAS A reaction in which an electrophile, E⁺, substitutes for a hydrogen on an aromatic ring: ArH + E⁺ → ArE + H⁺. The ring first attacks E⁺ using two of its six π electrons to form a new C–E bond and a resonance-stabilized, non-aromatic cyclohexadienyl cation (arenium ion); loss of H⁺ from that same carbon then restores full aromaticity.
Sulfonation: C₆H₆ + H₂SO₄ → C₆H₅SO₃H (benzenesulfonic acid) + H₂O. Alkylation: C₆H₆ + RX —AlCl₃→ C₆H₅R + HX. Acylation: C₆H₆ + RC(=O)X —AlCl₃→ C₆H₅C(=O)R + HX.
Building new C–C bonds on the ring
Alkylation
Forms a new C–C bond between an aromatic ring and an alkyl group, using AlCl₃ as a Lewis-acid catalyst.
Benzene + 2-chloropropane —AlCl₃→ Isopropylbenzene (Cumene) + HCl
Acylation
Treats an aromatic ring with an acid (acyl) chloride (a carboxylic acid derivative with –OH replaced by Cl) under AlCl₃. The product is a ketone, with the ring on one side of the carbonyl.
Benzene + Acetyl chloride (CH₃COCl) —AlCl₃→ Acetophenone + HCl
“Every interesting drug molecule contains a substituted benzene ring somewhere.” — quoted in the lecture as the practical payoff of mastering these substitution reactions.
Orientation & rate
Existing groups on a benzene ring influence further substitution in both orientation (which position reacts) and rate (how fast).
Ortho-para directors vs. meta directors
Ortho-para directors
Ortho-para attack forms a more stable cation than meta attack, so ortho-para products form faster.
Meta directors
Meta attack forms a more stable cation than ortho-para attack, so meta products form faster.
–OCH₃ is strongly activating & ortho-para directing

Anisole + Br₂ / CH₃COOH → 96% p-bromoanisole + 4% o-bromoanisole. Bromination of anisole proceeds many times faster than bromination of benzene — in fact –OCH₃ is so activating that no catalyst is necessary.
–NO₂ is strongly deactivating & meta directing
Nitrobenzene + HNO₃ / H₂SO₄ (100°C) → 93% m-dinitrobenzene, with less than 7% combined ortho + para product. Nitration of nitrobenzene proceeds many times slower than nitration of benzene.
Activating vs. deactivating directors
Activating directors

A resonance (electron-donating) effect for groups such as –NH₂, –OH, –OR delocalizes the positive charge on the cation intermediate, lowering the activation energy and making EAS faster. They direct ortho/para.
Deactivating directors
A resonance or inductive electron-withdrawing effect for groups such as –NO₂, –C=O, –SO₃H, –NR₃⁺, –CCl₃, –CF₃ decreases ring electron density, making EAS slower. They direct meta.
Effects of substituents on further EAS
Note: activating (and ortho/para-directing) groups generally have lone pairs that can participate in resonance stabilization of the cation intermediate.
Four rules to memorize

items: Substituents in which the atom bonded to the ring has an unshared pair of electrons

blocks.title: 2. All ortho-para directors are activating — except one class

blocks.x: The exceptions are the halogens, which are weakly deactivating despite being ortho-para directors. With excess reagent, disubstituted and trisubstituted rings are likely for activated (non-halogen) ortho-para directing rings.

blocks.title: 3. All other substituents are meta directing

blocks.x: Any group that is not an alkyl group, a phenyl group, or a lone-pair-bearing substituent directs new substitution to the meta position.

blocks.title: 4. All meta directors carry positive character on the ring-bonded atom

blocks.x: All meta-directing groups carry either a partial or a full positive charge on the atom directly bonded to the ring (e.g. the carbonyl carbon of –COR, the S of –SO₃H, or the fully positive N of –NR₃⁺), which destabilizes the ortho/para cation intermediates relative to the meta one.
